candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: If hell is an unpleasant separation from God, everyone there would seek divine rescue, apparently yielding universal salvation.
candidates.attributionBasis: The adversarial question beginning with “But” follows Jones's grace account and is answered directly by Jones in the same terminal row.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This challenges the coherence of self-chosen continuing exile by arguing that the experience of hell itself would motivate every occupant to leave.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Jones's claim that occupants can remain in hell while forgiveness and rescue remain available to anyone who asks.

candidates.contextSummary: Jones has just maintained that salvation rests on Christ's grace: those wanting forgiveness receive it, while those wanting isolation may remain isolated.

candidates.speaker: Michael Jones
candidates.proposition: God would grant grace to every soul in hell who calls upon Christ, so universalism follows if all souls actually do so.
candidates.attributionBasis: Jones begins with agreement and first-person expressions of hope, then supports the answer with Christian claims and cited scriptural passages.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The answer defines the defense's open route out of hell and explicitly accepts universal salvation under the skeptic's proposed psychological condition.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: O'Connor's contention that every person suffering separation from God would cry out to be rescued.

candidates.contextSummary: O'Connor has argued that any occupant experiencing hell as torment would seek God, creating pressure toward universal salvation rather than permanent exile.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: Jones's concessions entail universalism because anyone remaining in hell would either seek mercy or be excused for acting on false information.
candidates.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly frames this as the philosophical consequence of Jones's concessions, and Jones begins his answer in the terminal row.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This presents a dilemma intended to eliminate every morally permissible case of permanent hell under the proposed grace-and-self-exile account.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Jones's position that grace is granted to those who ask and that mistaken persons should receive mercy.

candidates.contextSummary: Jones has accepted that all souls would be saved if all called on Christ, while grounding that acceptance in divine love, the cross, and scripture.

candidates.speaker: Michael Jones
candidates.proposition: Universalism is possible and desirable but not guaranteed, because pride and preference can cause people to cling voluntarily to falsehood despite suffering.
candidates.attributionBasis: Jones identifies himself as a legal and hopeful universalist, then states his psychological disagreement with O'Connor's universalizing premise.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The reply preserves the possibility of enduring self-chosen exile by locating resistance in complex human motivation rather than unavailable grace or misinformation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: O'Connor's dilemma that every informed occupant would seek forgiveness and every misinformed occupant would merit mercy.

candidates.contextSummary: O'Connor has argued that correct information produces repentance while incorrect information warrants mercy, leaving no case in which anyone remains in hell.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: If hell or separation from God is humanity's consequence for sin, Jesus must undergo that same consequence to pay the price on humanity's behalf.
candidates.attributionBasis: O'Connor develops the objection in first-person skeptical language after Jones distinguishes Christ's harrowing of hell from suffering there.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection tests whether the atonement underlying the offered rescue from hell is substitutionally adequate on the defense's own account of sin's consequence.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Jones's claim that Jesus preached to the dead and defeated spiritual powers but did not go to hell in order to suffer.

candidates.contextSummary: Jones has said Jesus did not suffer in hell, that sin's wages are death rather than hell, and that the harrowing occurred after the resurrection.

candidates.speaker: Michael Jones
candidates.proposition: Sin's biblical consequences are death and exile, both of which Jesus undergoes through death and experienced separation from the Father on the cross.
candidates.attributionBasis: Jones answers by explicitly recalling the biblical consequence of sin and connects death, exile, forsakenness, and separation to the crucifixion.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the defense's account of how Christ bears sin's relevant penalty without needing to occupy the postmortem place called hell.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: O'Connor's objection that substitution requires Jesus to undergo hell and separation from God as sinners supposedly would.

candidates.contextSummary: O'Connor has argued that a substitute must experience the consequence assigned to unrepentant sinners and that Christianity does not place Jesus permanently in hell.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: The death described as sin's wages cannot merely be ordinary physical death and more plausibly denotes spiritual annihilation or a comparable fate.
candidates.attributionBasis: O'Connor immediately questions Jones's interpretation of death and contrasts universal physical mortality with a more distinctively spiritual consequence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move challenges the key exegetical premise used to claim that Jesus paid sin's full penalty through physical death and cross-bound separation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Jones's assertion that death, rather than hell, is the wages of sin and that Jesus bears death and separation on the cross.

candidates.contextSummary: Jones has distinguished the postmortem location of hell from the death and exile he says constitute sin's penalty and are borne at the crucifixion.

candidates.speaker: Michael Jones
candidates.proposition: Genesis portrays sin's penalty as eventual physical death through exclusion from the tree of life, which Christ reverses by restoring resurrection and eternal life.
candidates.attributionBasis: Jones signals uncertainty about the spiritual-death reading, then gives a sustained Genesis-based explanation ending with Christ and resurrection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument defends physical death as the relevant biblical penalty and explains how Christ's death and resurrection remedy humanity's loss of eternal life.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: O'Connor's suggestion that the wages of sin must mean spiritual annihilation rather than the physical death experienced by everyone.

candidates.contextSummary: O'Connor has pressed Jones to specify what kind of death sin earns, reasoning that ordinary mortality seems insufficiently distinctive as the consequence of sin.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: Temporary crucifixion followed by resurrection and heavenly exaltation appears too small a price to answer for the world's sins and humanity's supposed depravity.
candidates.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly asks whether Jesus pays the expected price and develops the comparative objection through the end of his turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This attacks the proportional adequacy of the atonement even if physical death is accepted, challenging the mechanism behind salvation from hell.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Jones's account that Christ takes sin's penalty of death and restores access to the Father, eternal life, and resurrection.

candidates.contextSummary: Jones has defended a Genesis-centered reading in which humans lose access to life through sin and Christ restores that access through death and resurrection.

candidates.speaker: Michael Jones
candidates.proposition: Christ's suffering is proportionate because sin produces an incomprehensibly severe rupture within the perfect unity and love of the infinite triune God.
candidates.attributionBasis: Jones directly answers the proportionality challenge by invoking divine infinity, Christ's full divinity, and severance between Father and Son.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response supplies the theological magnitude absent from a merely human crucifixion and thereby defends the sufficiency of Christ's atoning suffering.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: O'Connor's objection that crucifixion followed shortly by resurrection and exaltation is not a sufficiently great price for humanity's sins.

candidates.contextSummary: O'Connor has contrasted the severity attributed to humanity's sinful condition with Jesus's finite period of crucifixion before resurrection and eternal heavenly life.
